ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the attached image there is a room diagram with 2 rows and 4 columns. The upper row is numbered from left to right as 1, 2, 3, 4, and the lower row is numbered from left to right as 5, 6, 7, 8. The arrow on the left enters from outside into room 1 at the left end of the upper row, and the arrow on the right leaves from room 8 at the right end of the lower row. Observing the walls between adjacent rooms, door openings/gaps can be seen, so record these passable adjacent relationships as graph edges: 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 5-6, 6-7, 7-8, 1-5, 2-6, 3-7, 4-8. Reasoning: according to the method, take the room numbers as weights, start from room 1 and do DFS, with the state including the current position, the set of visited rooms, and the cumulative sum. One can only go along the above edges to unvisited rooms, and when reaching room 8, compare the total sum. One legal path is 1 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 3 -> 4 -> 8, with cumulative sum 1+5+6+7+3+4+8=34. It is also necessary to exclude larger cases: the sum of all room numbers is 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36; only if all 8 rooms can be traversed is it possible to exceed 34. But this 2-by-4 adjacency graph is a chessboard bipartite graph, and 1 and 8 are in the same class; an adjacent path containing 8 vertices must have its start and end in opposite classes, so it is impossible to traverse all 8 rooms from 1 to 8. Therefore at least one room must be omitted. The path must include the starting point 1 and the ending point 8, and the smallest number that can be omitted is 2, so theoretically the maximum is not more than 36-2=34. The above DFS path happens to reach 34, so the maximum result is 34.

method.method_draft: Model the diagram as a weighted graph and solve the longest simple entrance-to-exit path by exhaustive search or dynamic programming. First read the image: there are eight numbered rooms arranged as a 2-by-4 grid, with top row 1,2,3,4 and bottom row 5,6,7,8; the entrance arrow enters room 1 from the left, and the exit arrow leaves room 8 on the right. For every pair of adjacent rooms, inspect the shared wall and record an edge only where the drawn wall has an opening/gap. Then run a DFS from room 1: keep the set of already visited rooms, add the room number when entering a room, and recursively move only to unvisited adjacent rooms through recorded openings. Whenever room 8 is reached, allow exiting and compare the accumulated sum. The search should find the best admissible route, for example the visible route 1 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 3 -> 4 -> 8, with sum 34, and verify no other simple path has a larger sum.

First read the image: the rooms form a rectangular 2-by-4 grid with room 1 at the upper-left entrance side and room 8 at the lower-right exit side; movement between rooms is only through shared sides, never diagonally. One can only go along the above edges to unvisited rooms, and when reaching room 8, compare the total sum. One legal path is 1 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 3 -> 4 -> 8, with cumulative sum 1+5+6+7+3+4+8=34. It is also necessary to exclude larger cases: the sum of all room numbers is 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36; only if all 8 rooms can be traversed is it possible to exceed 34. But this 2-by-4 adjacency graph is a chessboard bipartite graph, and 1 and 8 are in the same class; an adjacent path containing 8 vertices must have its start and end in opposite classes, so it is impossible to traverse all 8 rooms from 1 to 8. Therefore at least one room must be omitted. The path must include the starting point 1 and the ending point 8, and the smallest number that can be omitted is 2, so theoretically the maximum is not more than 36-2=34. The above DFS path happens to reach 34, so the maximum result is 34.
